back: Oral (birth–1yr) → Anal (1–3yr) → Phallic (3–6yr) → Latency (6–12yr) → Genital (12+). Key: Latency is the ONLY stage NOT primarily sexual — sexual drives go dormant, replaced by social interests.
confusable_with: Erikson's psychosocial stages — Freud = psychoSEXUAL, Erikson = psychoSOCIAL

front: Erikson's 8 Psychosocial Stages (in order with approximate ages)
back:
1. Trust vs Mistrust (0–1yr)
2. Autonomy vs Shame & Doubt (1–3yr)
3. Initiative vs Guilt (3–6yr)
4. Industry vs Inferiority (6–12yr)
5. Identity vs Role Confusion (adolescence)
6. Intimacy vs Isolation (23–34yr)
7. Generativity vs Stagnation (35–60yr)
8. Integrity vs Despair (60+)
Key: Only theory covering the ENTIRE life span from birth to death.
confusable_with: Freud's 5 stages only go to age 12 (genital stage); Erikson's go to old age

back:
1. Sensorimotor (birth–2yr) — reflexes, object permanence
2. Preoperational (2–7yr) — egocentrism, animism, centration, symbolic play
3. Concrete Operations (7–11yr) — conservation, reversibility, logical thinking
4. Formal Operations (11+yr) — abstract thought, hypothetical reasoning
Memory trick: Stages always occur in same order; age may vary by culture.
confusable_with: Conservation belongs to Concrete Operations (not Preoperational); abstract thinking belongs to Formal Operations (not Concrete)

back: The understanding that a substance's weight, mass, and volume remain the same even if its shape changes. Mastered during Concrete Operations (ages 7–11). Order of mastery: Mass first → Weight → Volume. Memory trick: Conservation, Counting, Concrete all start with 'C'.
confusable_with: Object permanence (sensorimotor stage) — different concept; conservation is about substance constancy across shape changes

back: The understanding that objects continue to exist even when not visible. Develops during the Sensorimotor stage (~8 months+). A child without it thinks 'out of sight = out of mind.' Also called 'object constancy.'
confusable_with: Conservation — both involve object understanding but at different stages; object permanence = sensorimotor, conservation = concrete operations

back: The child's inability to view the world from anyone else's perspective. NOT selfishness — the child literally cannot take another's point of view. Classic example: child says 'the rain is following me.' Demonstrated by Piaget's 'Three Mountains Task.'
confusable_with: Centration — also preoperational, but centration = focusing on one feature of an object; egocentrism = inability to take others' perspectives

back: The tendency to focus exclusively on one salient feature of an object or situation while ignoring all others. Occurs in the Preoperational stage (ages 2–7). Example: child focuses only on a clown's red nose, ignoring all other features.
confusable_with: Egocentrism — both preoperational; egocentrism = perspective-taking failure, centration = attention narrowing to one feature

back: A child attributes lifelike qualities to inanimate objects (e.g., a rock is 'talking'). Occurs in the Preoperational stage (ages 2–7).
confusable_with: Egocentrism — both preoperational; animism = projecting life onto objects, egocentrism = inability to take others' views

back:
Assimilation: Taking in new information and fitting it into existing cognitive schemas.
Accommodation: Modifying existing schemas to handle new information that doesn't fit.
Equilibration (Equilibrium): The balance between assimilation and accommodation. When schemas can't process new info, 'disequilibrium' occurs, prompting accommodation.
confusable_with: These three work together; equilibration is the balancing mechanism, not a stage

front: Kohlberg's 3 Levels and 6 Stages of Moral Development
back:
Level 1 — Preconventional (premoral):
  Stage 1: Punishment/obedience orientation
  Stage 2: Naive hedonism ('if I'm nice, others will be nice to me')
Level 2 — Conventional (morality of conformity):
  Stage 3: Good boy/good girl orientation
  Stage 4: Authority, law & order
Level 3 — Postconventional (self-accepted principles):
  Stage 5: Social contract (democratically accepted law)
  Stage 6: Universal ethical principles
Key: Many people NEVER reach Level 3.
confusable_with: Piaget's moral stages (heteronomous vs autonomous) — Piaget has 2 stages, Kohlberg has 6 stages in 3 levels

back: A moral story used by Kohlberg to assess a person's stage of moral development. Key: It is the REASONING behind the decision (not the decision itself) that determines the moral stage. The dilemma involves a husband stealing a drug to save his dying wife.
confusable_with: It's not the answer (steal or not) that matters — it's the WHY. This distinguishes Kohlberg's method from simple rule-following.

back: When a child is severely traumatized, emotional development stops and the person becomes 'stuck' at that psychosexual stage. Physical and cognitive development may continue normally. The person returns to the safety of that stage under stress.
confusable_with: Regression — regression is returning to an earlier stage under stress AFTER having moved past it; fixation is never fully leaving the stage

back:
Oedipus Complex (boys): Unconscious wish to marry the mother, rage toward the father. Occurs during the Phallic stage (ages 3–5). Memory: Phallic and Oedipus both contain 'p.'
Electra Complex (girls): Analogous fantasy directed toward the opposite-sex parent.
Resolution: Child identifies with same-sex parent → superego/conscience is formed.
confusable_with: Occurs in the PHALLIC stage (not latency). Both involve fantasies about opposite-sex parent.

front: Freud's Structural Theory of the Mind: Id, Ego, Superego
back:
Id: 'Pleasure principle' — seat of sex and aggression; irrational, unconscious, chaotic. No sense of time or morality.
Ego: 'Reality principle' — logical, rational; mediates id impulses against reality.
Superego: Moralistic, idealistic portion; conscience. Corresponds to Berne's 'Parent ego state.'
Ego psychologists (like Erikson) emphasize the ego, not the id.
confusable_with: Erikson (ego psychologist) stresses ego control; Freud stressed the id/instincts

back:
British psychiatrist who saw bonding/attachment as having innate survival value. Key claims:
• Child must bond with an adult before age 3 for normal social development
• Failure to bond = 'object loss' → breeding ground for psychopathology
• Sequence of object loss: Protest → Despair → Detachment
Memory: Bowlby = Bonding (both start with 'B').
confusable_with: Harlow studied attachment in monkeys (contact comfort); Bowlby focused on human bonding theory

back: Demonstrated that 'contact comfort' is more important than food in attachment. Infant monkeys preferred terry-cloth mothers over wire mothers even when wire mothers provided milk. Monkeys raised in isolation developed autistic-like behavior. Concluded: Attachment is innate, not learned (Skinnerian food-based explanation rejected).
confusable_with: Bowlby — both deal with attachment; Harlow = animal experiments/contact comfort, Bowlby = human bonding theory

back:
Ethology: Study of animals' behavior in their natural environment (vs. comparative psychology = lab research).
Imprinting: Instinctual behavior in newborn animals to follow the first moving object encountered (normally the mother). Illustrates 'critical periods' — if certain behaviors are not learned during a specific window, they may never be learned.
confusable_with: Critical period vs sensitive period — critical period = behavior cannot be learned at all if missed; sensitive period = learning is easier during this window but possible later

back: The difference between what a child can do alone vs. what they can do with teacher guidance. Vygotsky argued developmental stages emerge through educational intervention (disagreed with Piaget's view that stages unfold naturally/biologically).
confusable_with: Piaget believed stages unfold naturally regardless of instruction; Vygotsky believed instruction drives development

back:
From lowest to highest:
1. Physiological (food, water, shelter)
2. Safety & Security
3. Love, Affection & Belonging
4. Self-Esteem
5. Self-Actualization
Key: Lower-order needs must be met before higher-order needs become motivating. Higher-order needs (non-physiological) are sometimes called 'metaneeds.' Maslow = Humanistic/'Third Force' psychology.
confusable_with: Self-esteem comes BEFORE self-actualization; love/belonging comes before self-esteem

back: Behavior is guided primarily by hereditary factors, but specific behaviors won't manifest until environmental stimuli are present and neural development is sufficiently mature. Associated with Arnold Gesell (who pioneered the one-way mirror for child observation). Contrasts with behaviorism, which emphasizes environment.
confusable_with: Nature vs nurture: maturationists lean toward nature/heredity; behaviorists lean toward nurture/environment

back:
Idiographic: Studies the individual in depth (e.g., Freud, Piaget — case study methods).
Nomothetic: Studies large groups to create general principles applicable to a population (e.g., behaviorism, DSM classification).
confusable_with: Easy to confuse directions: IDIOgraphic = IDIOsyncratic individual study; NOMOthetic = NORMS from groups

back: Each developmental stage emerges from the previous one in a fixed, systematic order. Associated with Erikson, Kohlberg, and Maslow. Also: contemporary definition includes that environmental factors can influence genetic expression.
confusable_with: Epigenetic ≠ genetics alone; it means stages build sequentially AND environment can influence genetic expression

back: Children reared in impersonal institutions who experienced maternal deprivation between 6–8 months of life cried more, had sleep difficulties, health problems, and great difficulty forming relationships. Called this 'anaclitic depression.'
confusable_with: Harlow's monkey studies showed similar results; Spitz studied human infants in institutional settings

back: Theory of child development focusing on the child's psychological 'birth' through separation from the mother. Calls the child's absolute dependence on the female caretaker 'symbiosis.' Difficulties in symbiotic relationship → adult psychosis.
confusable_with: Bowlby's attachment theory — both address early mother-child bonds, but Mahler focuses on symbiosis/individuation, Bowlby focuses on attachment security

back: Yale research: 80% of men studied experienced moderate to severe midlife crises. Levinson wrote 'Seasons of a Man's Life' and 'Seasons of a Woman's Life.' Viewed midlife crisis as somewhat positive — avoiding it can lead to stagnation in one's 50s. Midlife crisis typically: men ages 35–45, women about 5 years earlier.
confusable_with: Erikson's Generativity vs Stagnation (ages 35–60) covers similar developmental territory; Levinson's model is more focused on adult transitions

back:
Proposed developmental tasks at each life stage:
• Infancy & early childhood: walking, eating solid foods
• Middle childhood (6–12): learning to get along with peers, developing conscience
• Adolescence (12–18): preparing for marriage, economic career
• Early adulthood (19–30): selecting mate, starting family
• Middle age (30–60): civic responsibility, guiding teenagers
• Later maturity (60+): adjusting to retirement, death of spouse
confusable_with: Erikson's stages — both cover full life span; Havighurst focuses on tasks/skills, Erikson focuses on psychosocial crises

front: Robert Perry — Dualistic vs Relativistic Thinking
back:
Perry's model of adult cognitive development in college students:
• Dualistic thinking (common in teens): things are good/bad, right/wrong — black-and-white, no ambiguity. Students assume the professor has 'the answer.'
• Relativistic thinking (adulthood): not everything is right or wrong; answers exist relative to situations. Multiple worldviews are possible.
confusable_with: Robert Kegan also studies adult cognitive development; Kegan focuses on interpersonal/constructive development, Perry focuses on epistemological development

front: Robert Kegan — Constructive Model of Development
back: Individuals construct reality throughout the life span. 6 stages: incorporative, impulsive, imperial, interpersonal, institutional, interindividual. Concept of 'holding environment': a therapeutic space where clients can make meaning in the face of crisis and find new direction.
confusable_with: Robert Perry — both study adult development; Perry = epistemological (how we know), Kegan = meaning-making/interpersonal construction

front: Harry Stack Sullivan — Interpersonal Relations Theory
back: Proposed stages: infancy, childhood, juvenile era, preadolescence, early adolescence, late adolescence. Similar to Erikson in that biological determinism is less important than interpersonal and sociocultural factors. Key focus: social influences on development.
confusable_with: Erikson — both emphasize social/interpersonal factors over biology; Sullivan focuses on interpersonal relationships, Erikson on psychosocial crises

back: Occurs in Erikson's Stage 5: Identity vs Role Confusion (adolescence). Adolescents experiment with various roles trying to discover who they are. Failure to integrate roles into a single self-concept = role confusion = identity crisis. Term 'identity crisis' was coined by Erikson.
confusable_with: Midlife crisis (Levinson) — different developmental period; identity crisis = adolescence, midlife crisis = 35–45

back: Ages 35–60. Generativity = productive concern for establishing and guiding the next generation; includes raising a family, creative work, career. Failure = self-centeredness/self-absorption. Memory: 'Generativity' sounds like 'generation' — planning for the next generation.
confusable_with: Integrity vs Despair (Stage 8, age 60+): that stage is about reviewing one's life; generativity is about being productive for others

back: Begins approximately age 11–12. Characteristics: abstract thought, hypothetical/deductive reasoning, ability to consider multiple hypotheses simultaneously. Key: Abstract concepts of time and distance (e.g., 'what was life like 500 years ago?') can only be understood in this stage. Many people never fully reach this stage.
confusable_with: Concrete Operations — can think logically but only about concrete/tangible things; Formal Operations = abstract and hypothetical

back: Bodily development proceeds from head to tail (head to foot). The head of the fetus develops earlier than the legs. Development begins at conception (not birth).
confusable_with: Proximodistal development (center outward) — different developmental principle

back: Nature = heredity/genetic makeup. Nurture = environment. The classic debate about which has greater impact on development. Modern view: both play significant roles. Behaviorists (Skinner) lean toward nurture/environment; maturationists (Gesell) lean toward nature/heredity.
confusable_with: Empiricism vs organicism: empiricists (behaviorists) believe change is measurable via environment; organicists believe change is internal/qualitative

front: Piaget's Moral Development: Heteronomous vs Autonomous
back:
Heteronomous morality (ages 4–7): Rules are absolutes handed down by authority; violations automatically result in punishment.
Autonomous morality (begins ~age 10): Rules are relative and can be changed; intentions matter, not just consequences.
Kohlberg expanded on Piaget's moral development work.
confusable_with: Kohlberg's 3 levels — Piaget has 2 stages of moral development, Kohlberg expanded to 6 stages

back: Pattern in which repeated exposure to uncontrollable situations leads a person to believe they have no control over their environment, even when control is possible. Associated with depression. Seligman demonstrated this by giving inescapable electric shocks to harnessed dogs — they didn't try to escape even when the harness was removed.
confusable_with: Seligman is associated with BOTH learned helplessness (problem) AND positive psychology (solution/strengths focus)

front: Suicide Statistics — Key Facts for NCE
back:
• Males complete suicide more often; females attempt more often (males use more lethal methods, e.g., firearms)
• Suicide = 2nd or 3rd leading cause of death in teens
• U.S. suicide rate ≈ 12/100,000 overall
• Lowest rate: African American females (≈2/100,000)
• Suicidal risk may INCREASE as depression begins to LIFT
• MMPI-2 and Rorschach are NOT good predictors of suicide
• Always take suicide threats seriously
confusable_with: Adolescent suicide rate — suicide is concerning but statistically rare compared to other causes of teen death

back:
Study of middle-class boys (ages 10–12). Key finding: Children with HIGH self-esteem:
• Were punished just as often as low self-esteem kids
• Had MORE rules, not fewer
• Punishment emphasized bad BEHAVIOR, not bad child
• Parents were democratic — explained rules and listened to arguments
confusable_with: Common misconception: permissiveness raises self-esteem. Coopersmith found clear limits + democratic explanation = high self-esteem

back:
Reviewed literature and found few differences attributable to genetics/biology. Key findings:
• Girls: better verbal skills, better at reading nonverbal cues at any age, use more feeling words by age 2, smile more
• Boys: better visual-perceptual skills, more physically active and aggressive
• Math advantage for males (if any) doesn't appear until high school/college
• Most sex-role differences are due to socialization (child-rearing), not biology
• Exception: male aggression may have a biological component
confusable_with: Sandra Bem — also studied gender; Bem focused on androgyny and gender stereotyping, Maccoby/Jacklin studied actual sex differences in behavior

back: Caused by chromosomal abnormality (extra chromosome 21 = three copies). Characterized by broad facial profile, short stature, IQ typically 50–80 (100 is average). Intelligence can be improved by early intervention, environment, and education. Other genetic conditions to know: PKU, Klinefelter's syndrome, Turner's syndrome.
confusable_with: Klinefelter's (XXY male — extra X chromosome) vs Turner's (female, no sex hormones) — all are genetic/chromosomal

back: The ability to mentally reverse an action — understanding that an operation can be undone. Example: understanding that water poured from one container back to the original returns to original volume. Mastered in the Concrete Operations stage along with conservation.
confusable_with: Conservation — related but distinct: conservation = substance quantity unchanged, reversibility = mental undoing of an action

front: Conformity and Peer Pressure by Developmental Stage
back: Conformity peaks in early adolescence (early teens, approximately age 13). This is a key NCE/CPCE fact — a 13-year-old is most likely to conform to peer pressure compared to college students, adult professionals, or older adolescents.
confusable_with: Identity crisis (adolescence) — conformity peaks in early teens, while identity formation spans broader adolescence

back:
Oral character: Fixation at oral stage → excessive dependency, smoking, alcoholism, overeating (all involve the mouth).
Anal retentive character: Fixation at anal stage (retention phase) → stingy, orderly, stubborn, cheap.
Anal expulsive: messy, disorganized, reckless.
confusable_with: Oral = mouth-related behaviors (drinking, smoking); Anal retentive = holding on (money, emotions)

back:
Manifest content: The dream as experienced and remembered by the dreamer — the surface story.
Latent content: The hidden, unconscious meaning of the dream. Freudians consider latent content far more therapeutically important.
confusable_with: Manifest = surface/visible (like manifest on a ship's cargo list); Latent = hidden/latent (like the latency stage where sexuality is hidden)

back:
Eros: The life instinct (libido — sexual/creative energy that sustains life).
Thanatos: The death/self-destructive instinct (aggression turned inward). Both are drives housed in the id.
confusable_with: Libido is often equated only with sexuality, but technically it is the energy of Eros (life instinct)

front: Stranger Anxiety & Depth Perception in Infants
back:
• Stranger anxiety develops at approximately 8 months (child can now discriminate familiar from unfamiliar faces).
• Depth perception research: Eleanor Gibson's 'visual cliff' apparatus — by 6 months most infants will NOT cross a simulated drop-off, suggesting depth perception is innate.
confusable_with: Object permanence also develops around 8 months — distinguish: stranger anxiety = social recognition, object permanence = understanding objects exist when hidden

back:
Empiricism: Grew from John Locke; only objective, measurable facts count; views development as quantitative changes. Forerunner of behaviorism.
Organicism: Views development as qualitative changes (stages); associated with Gestalt psychology and organicists like Kurt Goldstein. Emphasizes holistic model; no mind-body distinction.
confusable_with: Quantitative = empiricism/behaviorism; Qualitative = organicism/stage theorists

back:
Founder of Individual Psychology. Key concepts:
• Inferiority complex: Everyone starts life feeling inferior (small, weak child) and compensates.
• Organ inferiority: Striving to compensate for physical weaknesses.
• Social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl): A healthy person has concern for the community.
• Adler emphasized birth order's role in personality.
confusable_with: Freud — Adler was originally a Freudian disciple but broke away; Adler rejected the primacy of sexuality, emphasizing social factors and inferiority instead

back:
• Secondary school counseling/guidance was popular since early 1900s (Frank Parsons)
• Elementary school counseling gained momentum in the 1960s (NOT early 1900s)
• In the 1980s, some state departments of education made elementary school counselors mandatory
• Middle school/junior high counseling is even MORE recent than elementary
• Approximately 260,000 school counselors in the United States
• Only organized profession focused purely on prevention and developmental standpoints
confusable_with: Frank Parsons → secondary/vocational guidance (early 1900s); elementary counseling didn't take off until the 1960s
